paragraphs.text: Today the athlete of the whole world has come to us, as he does every year. He has come to us, that extraordinary contender, equal in honor to the angels: struck many times by the devil, and many times given testimony by God; wounded many times by the devil, and receiving many prizes from the angels who watched; scourged many times by the enemy, and shown to the world by God as a great crowned victor. For God himself, speaking with him, said: "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?" Who, then, can praise such a champion as he deserves? Who will dare to weave prizes worthy of his heroic deeds? Who will try to set out on a boundless sea of praises? No one in his right mind would ever dare to cross the open sea on human feet, and in the same way none of the wise and most accomplished teachers will ever try to tell his hearers the praises that this noble and thrice-blessed soul deserves. For his achievements surpass all human wisdom, and his wrestling bouts surpass every crown. So we need the tongue of an angel, so that by touching that perfume-casket with the tips of our fingers, so to speak, we may fill the whole church at once. For if we only try to touch Job's vessel and stir it a little, the church is at once filled with the fragrance of the perfume. Let us hear, then, what the story says about him: "In all these things that befell him, Job did not sin at all with his lips before the Lord." Do you see a testimony that stirs the angels to praise? Do you see a testimony that puts the devil and his schemes to shame? "In all these things that befell him he did not sin at all." This testimony of God gladdens its hearers in every church like precious perfume. O precious vessel, laid up in one place in Arabia, yet sending out the fragrance of its perfume through the whole world! O vessel struck by the devil with countless stones and blows and arrows, yet never spilling its perfume! The devil toiled hard to shatter the vessel and destroy the perfume of piety. He strove to dim the fragrance of the perfume with the stench of the wounds, and indeed Job's body did stink from his festering wounds. But the vessel survived its wounds and the perfume was not lost, so that we too may fittingly say to him: "Your name is perfume poured out." We must, then, set the athlete before us naked, as he was when he wrestled. Then, gazing on that marvelous image, we may be fully convinced by the very nature of the events of why God allowed this drama to be staged: he wished to show the devil that he has righteous men on earth, men who are no longer deceived by flattery as Adam was, but are crowned through countless torments and scourges. "Apostate," he says, "you are proud because you deceived Adam and flattered the woman, and so cast him out of paradise. Look, here is a man who has lived without the commandments of Scripture and has fulfilled the unwritten law of nature with his mind. Bring on countless blandishments, countless flatteries, countless torments, and see whether you can shake this most excellent soul. Yes, you cast the first man out of paradise. Look now: try, if you can, to trip up this athlete, even from his dunghill." But, if you will, let us go back a little to the beginning of the story itself: "There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And that man was blameless, righteous, God-fearing and true, and kept himself from every evil deed." Adam too was like this before he was persuaded by the woman. That is why this man is not persuaded by his wife: so that he may not become like Adam. Adam was clothed in incorruption, as the one who formed him knows, and because he was persuaded by the woman he became naked and was condemned. Job was naked and was not persuaded by his wife, and because he was not persuaded by his wife he was clothed with the crown of the angels. Adam was persuaded by the woman, and so he fell from the delight of paradise, made the earth a mother of thorns, and inherited death. Job was not persuaded by his wife, and so he was freed from the dunghill and the wounds and inherited the kingdom of heaven. Adam, making his defense to God, said: "The woman you gave me, she gave it to me, and I ate." O defense that admits no excuse! "She said, 'Eat'; I said, 'Do not eat.' Why, then, did you listen to the woman and disobey God?" But blessed Job was not like that. What did he do? He rebuked her, saying: "You have spoken like one of the foolish women." "There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job." Why did it name the land? For your sake, so that you may learn that the company of sinners cannot make a righteous man sin. Rather, the will of the godly must keep its resolve steady and firm. For this land of Arabia was a home of wicked and corrupt people. All of them were lawless, all hateful to God, all profane, all arrogant; they were descendants of Esau and flourished in their sins. Yet so great a sea of ungodliness could not quench the lamp of piety, and so great a land of evils could not choke the beauty of endurance. That is why the devil tried to attack him. Why? Because he saw that Job was rich in almsgiving more than in money. Hear him say, and truthfully: "I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame"; and again, "I wept over the helpless, and I groaned when I saw a man in distress." And he was rich not only in words but also in deeds, proving to be a whole treasury of kindness for those in need. For what does he say elsewhere? "No one in need went out of my house with an empty lap; the mouth of the widow blessed me; and the shoulders of the poor were warmed with the fleece of my sheep." So it is clear that he was rich in every way, a whole treasury: in words, in deeds, in almsgiving, in protecting the poor and in helping those in need. But see what the devil does. First he snatches away all Job's possessions, and last of all he takes his children. First he took the herds of camels; he took the flocks of sheep, the great number of donkeys, the huge herd of oxen. He took everything away, and last of all the children. Why? Now pay very close attention. First he took all Job's possessions, and then his children. He took the inheritance and then destroyed the heirs, so that he might strike him in every way, through his children as well. He began by destroying Job's property, and he began by seizing the inheritance while the heirs were still alive, so that, while the sons and daughters were still standing, the righteous man might be dealt a mortal blow of despair by the loss of his possessions. For the evil demon reckoned that if the children died first, Job would not even feel the loss of his possessions. But the truly adamantine and noble athlete was struck many times and crowned through it all; he took many arrows and shot the devil down with those very arrows; he was armed with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. He did not suffer distress, he did not weep, he was not shaken. He did not bend at the loss of his possessions, nor was he robbed of his piety by the death of his children. Instead he stood like an unshakable tower, rooted and founded below in the earth and made secure up to the very vaults of heaven. The first messenger came and said to Job: "The oxen were plowing in their yokes, and raiders came and carried them off, and killed the servants with swords." While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said to Job: "Fire fell from heaven and burned up your sheep, and devoured the shepherds as well."

See what the devil does. He saw Job standing nobly through the first and second blows, not shaken at all by his torments, attacked yet not wounded, and so he devises a plan like this: he hurls fire from the air, so that it might seem to be sent down from heaven. Then Job would think that God was fighting him from heaven, and would blaspheme God for fighting him so unjustly when he had committed no sin. "Fire," he says, "fell from heaven and devoured your sheep and the shepherds." While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said to Job: "The horsemen formed three companies against us, surrounded the camels and carried them off, and killed the servants with swords." But through all these things blessed Job stood like an immovable pillar, like an unshaken tower, like an invincible contender, unbending and unyielding, striking rather than struck. For when someone toils uselessly, fighting hard and gaining nothing, battling often and never prevailing at all, he is really the one who takes the lashes for his vain labors. "While he was still speaking, another messenger came." The war is unceasing, but futile for the one who wages it; the arrows come thicker, but the prizes grow brighter. He does not let Job breathe even for an hour, so that the wrestler's innate piety will not lead him to some wise thought. He shot all his arrows and did not conquer the athlete; he emptied his quiver, but was not emptied of his pain. "Let those who act lawlessly without cause be put to shame." So he too turned back humbled and ashamed, after wrestling hard and being defeated at every point. For he sent his attacks against the shepherds, against the herdsmen, against the sheep, against the camels, against the sons, against the daughters, against the house, against the body; through friends, through servants, through worms, through wounds, through oozing pus. He used up everything, and did not undo Job's piety. He dug through the wall, and did not empty the treasury. The tyrant of the world brandished every sword he had: fire, swords, rubble, captivity, blood. He strained every one of them, and only made the athlete braver. That is why the prophet cried out, saying: "The swords of the enemy have failed utterly." And perhaps it is also said to him: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads." He took all Job's money, his possessions, his property. And what did the last messenger say? "While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a wind came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell on your children, and they died." And so that you may learn, beloved, that it was not a man who announced these things to Job, but the devil himself disguised in human form, examine it very closely: "While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking with their eldest brother, suddenly a wind came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell on your children, and they died." Tell me, how do you know that it came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house? You are a man; how did you see the wind? With what eyes did you see it? And how did the wind strike the four corners? If you are a man and were inside the house, the house would surely have buried you too; and if you were outside, how did you see what was happening inside? But if you are a spirit, show us who you are, and do not disguise yourself in human form. "While your sons," he says, "and your daughters were eating and drinking with their eldest brother." See how full of understanding and wisdom blessed Job was, and how he safeguarded the love among his children. For he reckoned that Cain and Abel were two brothers, the only ones in the world, with no cause for war, since the whole earth lay open to both of them in common. Yet Cain, envying the honor given to Abel, rose up and murdered his brother. That is why blessed Job offered sacrifice to God every day for their hidden sins, rising early in the morning and saying: "Perhaps my sons have thought evil against God in their hearts." And because of what might arise between them, whether a word or a quarrel, he had them eat together every day. He thought that even if they had some petty grievance against one another, the table and the sharing of bread would turn them back to friendship and drive out any malice that had arisen, for he knew that a constant table would resolve all the troubles that came up among them. But the devil, who hates the good, watched for just such an occasion to destroy the children, who had done no wrong. At midday, when they were all gathered together, when they were joining in peace, he unleashed against them a war without truce. They were forging friendship; he was sharpening a sword. They were building love; he was overturning the house. And in that very hour the house became a tomb, the table a ship of disaster, the shepherd's fold a shipwreck, and everything a prey to wild beasts. What, then, did that noble man do? He was not confounded; he did not collapse. What shall I praise in him? What words will suffice? What labor will be enough to tell such a story? O noble and blessed soul! O great endurance that none can surpass! Truly, beloved, I am confounded in soul and troubled in conscience, even as I see Job crowned. Indeed, I am more confounded in soul now, seeing him as a crowned victor, than he was then, seeing the disaster of his children before his eyes. I am confounded in soul, and I think you feel the same. I do not know how to tell so great a tragedy, even though the crowning flourish of my praises is on my tongue. When parents according to the flesh have a son in the grip of his last breaths, they sit around him, listen to his last words, clasp his hands, make arrangements for what they never expected, and kiss his mouth with a father's last kisses. Then, when the child has given up his soul as the one who gave it commanded, the parents lay him out: they straighten his arms, close his eyes, set his head straight, stretch out his feet, wash him, clothe him in fitting grave-clothes, and so console themselves in their misfortune. But what of this noble athlete? He went to the house that in one and the same hour had become both house and tomb, banquet and heap of rubble, feast and mourning. He dug around and searched for his children's limbs, and he found wine and blood, bread and a hand, an eye and dust. He would pick up now a hand, now a foot; at another time he would pull out a head along with the earth and the stones and the timbers; now part of a belly, at another time the entrails, mixed up with the rubble. And that contender, tall as heaven, sat there, looking at his children's torn limbs. He sat fitting limb to limb, hand to arm, joining head to chest and knees to thighs. For this was not a single calamity among many, but a catastrophe beyond all words, brought about by the working and tyranny of the devil. So Job sat, that truly enduring adamant, the blessed one, sorting out his children's limbs, so that he would not join the girls' limbs to the boys' limbs, nor fit a male form onto a girl's limbs. O noble soul, surpassing even the praise of the angels! Why? Because in all these things that befell him Job did not sin at all before the Lord. Instead, in return for all of them, he offered God a whole thanksgiving in place of a sacrifice, saying: "May the name of the Lord be blessed," now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
